title: Dates and Times
intro: The `datetime` module has `date` (a calendar day), `datetime` (a day plus a time) and `timedelta` (a length of time). Subtract two dates to get a `timedelta`; add a `timedelta` to move forward or back. `strftime` turns a date into text and `datetime.strptime` reads text back into a date. These exercises use fixed dates, because `datetime.now()` changes every time you run it.

questions.prompt: Format codes start with `%`: `%Y` year, `%m` month number, `%d` day, `%H:%M` hours and minutes, `%A` weekday name, `%b` short month name.
questions.exampleCode:
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

release = date(2025, 9, 1)
print(release.strftime("%A %d %b %Y"))   # Monday 01 Sep 2025
print(release + timedelta(weeks=2))       # 2025-09-15

kickoff = datetime.strptime("2025-09-01 14:30", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
print(kickoff.hour, kickoff.minute)       # 14 30

questions.prompt: Create `launch` as the date 14 March 2025, and set `weekday_name` to its weekday name (like `"Monday"`) using `strftime`.
questions.solution:
from datetime import date

launch = date(2025, 3, 14)
weekday_name = launch.strftime("%A")

tests.name: date
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert launch == _d(2025, 3, 14), 'launch should be date(2025, 3, 14).'

tests.name: weekday
tests.code: assert weekday_name == 'Friday', 'weekday_name should be the full weekday name of launch.'

questions.explanation: `%A` gives the full weekday name; `%a` gives the short one, like `Fri`.

questions.prompt: 2024 is a leap year. What does this print?
questions.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

print(date(2024, 2, 28) + timedelta(days=2))
questions.explanation: 28 Feb + 2 days skips over 29 Feb and lands on 1 March. `timedelta` handles month lengths and leap years for you.

questions.prompt: Write `days_until(deadline, today)` that returns how many days are left until `deadline`, as a whole number (negative if it has passed).

tests.name: future
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert days_until(_d(2025, 12, 25), _d(2025, 12, 1)) == 24, 'From 1 to 25 December is 24 days.'

tests.name: past
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert days_until(_d(2025, 1, 1), _d(2025, 1, 11)) == -10, 'A passed deadline gives a negative number.'

tests.name: across years
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert days_until(_d(2026, 1, 2), _d(2025, 12, 30)) == 3, 'It should work across a new year.'

questions.hint: Subtracting two dates gives a `timedelta`; it has a `.days` attribute.
questions.explanation: `deadline - today` is a `timedelta`, and `.days` is its length in whole days.

questions.hint: Day comes first here, and the year has four digits.
questions.explanation: `%d/%m/%Y` is day/month/four-digit year. `%M` (capital) is *minutes*, not months, and `%y` is a two-digit year.

questions.prompt: The meeting is on **3 November 2025 at 18:30**, but `meeting` comes out as 11 March. Fix the format string.
questions.starterCode:
from datetime import datetime

meeting = datetime.strptime("2025-11-03 18:30", "%Y-%d-%m %H:%M")
questions.solution:
from datetime import datetime

meeting = datetime.strptime("2025-11-03 18:30", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")

tests.name: value
tests.code:
from datetime import datetime as _dt
assert meeting == _dt(2025, 11, 3, 18, 30), 'meeting should be 3 November 2025, 18:30.'

questions.hint: Look at the order of the parts in the text: year, then month, then day.
questions.explanation: The format string must follow the text's order exactly. Swapping `%d` and `%m` reads the day as the month.

questions.prompt: Fill in the method that turns a `timedelta` into a number of seconds, so `minutes` is the length of the workshop.
questions.template:
from datetime import datetime

start = datetime(2025, 5, 1, 9, 15)
end = datetime(2025, 5, 1, 11, 45)
minutes = (end - start).___() / 60
questions.explanation: `total_seconds()` counts the whole duration. (`.seconds` alone ignores whole days — a common trap.)

questions.prompt: Write `age(birthday, on)` that returns how old someone born on `birthday` is on the date `on`, in whole years.

tests.name: before birthday
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert age(_d(2000, 6, 15), _d(2025, 6, 14)) == 24, 'The day before the birthday they are still 24.'

tests.name: on birthday
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert age(_d(2000, 6, 15), _d(2025, 6, 15)) == 25, 'On the birthday they turn 25.'

tests.name: leap day
tests.code:
from datetime import date as _d
assert age(_d(2004, 2, 29), _d(2025, 2, 28)) == 20 and age(_d(2004, 2, 29), _d(2025, 3, 1)) == 21, 'Someone born on 29 February turns 21 on 1 March 2025.'

questions.hint: Subtract the years, then take one away if this year's birthday hasn't happened yet. Comparing `(month, day)` tuples does that check.
questions.explanation: Dividing the days by 365 goes wrong around leap years; comparing month and day is exact.

questions.prompt: A datetime can carry a time zone. What does this print?
questions.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta

utc = datetime(2025, 1, 1, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(utc.astimezone(timezone(timedelta(hours=-5))).isoformat())
questions.explanation: `astimezone` shows the same moment in another zone. `isoformat()` writes the offset at the end, so the text can't be misread.

questions.prompt: A course meets every 7 days starting on Monday 6 January 2025. Build `sessions`, a list of the first four dates formatted like `Mon 06 Jan`.
questions.starterCode:
from datetime import date, timedelta

sessions = []
questions.solution:
from datetime import date, timedelta

first = date(2025, 1, 6)
sessions = [(first + timedelta(days=7 * i)).strftime("%a %d %b") for i in range(4)]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert sessions == ['Mon 06 Jan', 'Mon 13 Jan', 'Mon 20 Jan', 'Mon 27 Jan'], 'sessions should be four weekly dates like Mon 06 Jan.'

questions.hint: Add `timedelta(days=7 * i)` for `i` in `range(4)` and format with `%a %d %b`.
questions.explanation: Building dates by adding `timedelta`s avoids working out month ends yourself.
